schools.summary: Gill marvels that a man in Job's misery has such keenness of spirit, dealing in irony and satire and laughing outright at his antagonist.
Henry: Job, in pain, banters Bildad and makes merry with the impertinency of a speech its author fancied made him both oracle and orator.
Ellicott: Job had virtually said the same himself (ch. 9:2; 14:4), so makes no further comment but asks how Bildad has helped him or any helpless man.
Clarke reads the chapter's shape: reproof of the friends' want of wisdom and feeling (vv.1-4), then a display of God's power and wisdom in creation (vv.5-14).
Gill reads the verse of God: Bildad plays a poor advocate, picturing the Almighty as powerless and needing help, counsel, and an arm, when he is omnipotent and all-wise.
Clarke hears irony at the friends' feebleness ('ye could not give what ye did not possess'), backed by the Chaldee's 'why pretend to give succour when thou art without strength?'
Henry's cui bono: Job has done God no service; God needs no such help, nor accepts service offered from a spirit of contention rather than a regard to his glory.

debates.question: Who is the one 'without power' that Bildad has failed to help?

sides.position: God, whom Bildad officiously defends as though heaven needed an advocate
Job, or any afflicted man, whom Bildad's barren comfort left unstrengthened

themes: how hast thou helped the powerless

schools.summary: Gill lets Job grant he is the fool they take him for, only to ask what counsel Bildad has actually given — a miserable part acted under the character of counsellor.
Ellicott corrects the rendering: 'how hast thou plentifully declared sound knowledge?' — Job bantering Bildad's conceit of a fulness of solid wisdom in few words.
Henry: Bildad, fond of his own notions, thought he declared the thing as it is; but of God's glory we see through a glass darkly, and he spoke scantily beside the vast subject.

themes: counselled him that hath no wisdom
declaring the thing as it is

schools.summary: Gill: does Bildad think he speaks to an ignorant man? Job knows as much of God and more; and to an afflicted man one should discourse of mercy and the promised Redeemer, not of majesty.

Clarke (with Good and Stock) reads the rest of the chapter as Job's ironic sample of the friends' borrowed harangues, which he outdoes in sublimity; Wesley: for whose instruction, and who inspired this?
Ellicott: was it not to one who had said the same himself — his own breath returned to him? — and Job turns to show the under-world too declares God's glory.

debates.question: Is the hymn of vv.5-14 Job's own adoring praise or an ironic parody of the friends' borrowed eloquence?

sides.position: an ironic parody, Job outdoing the friends at the harangues they had pillaged from others
Job's own sincere natural theology, showing that the whole universe declares God's glory

outliers.note: Following Good and Stock, treats vv.5-14 as a deliberate ironic imitation of the friends' plagiarised eloquence, and infers from their falsehood that their spirit was not the Spirit of God.

themes: to whom hast thou uttered words

schools.summary: Gill takes the Rephaim ('dead things') for lifeless things formed under the waters — grains of corn, metals, minerals, pearls, corals (Aben Ezra, Ben Gersom).

Wesley allows either the lifeless treasures of the deep or dead men, the worst of them, groaning under the waters; Clarke denies 'dead things,' referring the word to the drowned antediluvian giants or sea-monsters.

Ellicott: the Rephaim, aboriginal race by the Dead Sea, stand for the dead/nether world, 'pierced' or 'trembling' with terror; Keil and Delitzsch: the bloodless shades below writhe when God's majesty is felt.
Henry joins the readings — vast sea-creatures (Patrick) and the drowned giants of the old world (Mede), whose ruin typifies hell laid naked before God.

debates.question: What are the 'dead things' (Rephaim) formed under the waters?

sides.position: lifeless, inanimate treasures of the deep — corn, metals, minerals, pearls, corals
the trembling shades of the dead in the nether world
the drowned antediluvian giants (or sea-monsters) of a former world

themes: dead things formed under the waters
God's dominion over the hidden deep

schools.summary: Gill lets 'hell' bear its full range — the place of the damned, Hades, or the grave — all naked and open to the eye of God.
Keil and Delitzsch set the movement: Bildad praised God's rule in heaven's heights; Job extends it to the depths, so neither sea nor realm of shades bars God — Sheol bare, the abyss uncovered.

Clarke: Sheol the place of the dead, Abaddon of the destroyer; quotes Virgil's Tartarus but denies the sacred writers countenance the fable; Wesley: hell, that utter darkness, lies open in God's presence.
Henry: hell and destruction may mean the grave and its buried, still under God's eye (a ground for resurrection faith), or the place of the damned always before the Lord (Prov. 15:11).
Henry marvels that the globe rests on no pillars yet is poised by its own weight ('ponderibus librata suis'), upheld by God's word; man could not hang a feather on nothing.

Keil and Delitzsch take 'the north' of the northern sky (not the earth's north, against Hirzel and Ewald), since 'stretcheth out' is always used of the heavens; Ellicott hears a remarkable anticipation of science in 'hangeth the earth upon nothing.'

Wesley: 'the north' is the northern heaven, put for the whole visible sky; the earth hangs on no props but God's power; Clarke notes 'the empty place' is tohu (Gen. 1:2) and the Chaldee's softening 'upon the waters.'
Gill likewise reads the northern hemisphere expanded over the empty place.

debates.question: Does 'the north' mean the northern sky or the northern part of the earth?

sides.position: the northern quarter of the heavens, put for the visible sky
the northern part of the earth
holders: Hirzel (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Ewald (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

outliers.note: Reads 'hangeth the earth upon nothing' as a remarkable anticipation of the discoveries of science — Job describing the globe with scientific accuracy three thousand years ago as a proof of divine power.

schools.summary: Henry: God binds the waters as in a bag, and the cloud is not rent, else it would pour like a spout; instead the rain distils drop by drop in mercy to the earth.
Gill: the clouds, God's chariots of exhaled vapour, are thin, yet hold bound so heavy a body of water — a thing tied up in a sack or a coat's skirt.

Keil and Delitzsch: God holds the rolled-up water-masses together so they do not burst — the laws of rain are of his appointment; Ellicott: a treasury of water above the sky, kept in apparent defiance of gravitation (cf. Gen. 1:7).
Clarke supplies the mechanism: vapour condensed to floating cloud, further condensed by wind or the electric fluid till too heavy, falls as rain — the cloud 'rent under them.'

themes: the laws of rain appointed by God

schools.summary: Gill: the throne is the heaven of heavens, its 'face' the starry and airy heavens, sometimes so curtained with cloud that not even its outward appearance is seen.

Wesley reads the veiling as mercy to weak eyes, lest God's glory dazzle us; Clarke: through all these effects the great Agent stays personally undiscoverable, dwelling in light unapproachable, or the words mean the sky darkened before rain.
Henry makes it a lesson in faith: God hides the dazzling face of his throne that we may live by faith not sight — no fair trial if it were as visible now as in the great day.

Keil and Delitzsch: the verb 'holdeth back' means to take hold of or fasten together, God closing over the throne's face; Ellicott: 'he covereth the face of his throne, spreading his rack of cloud upon it.'
Henry: God bounds the sea that it may not cover the earth, unmoved till day and night end — his dominion over the waters (Jer. 5:22) and his care of the earth's inhabitants.
Ellicott and Keil read the bound as a circle described on the face of the waters unto the confines of light and darkness — the perfect circle of the sea's horizon.
Clarke offers the same horizon-circle ('the completion of light with darkness'), perhaps the twilight's sky-blue tint, or God circumscribing the waters till day and night, i.e. time, end.
Gill weighs the waters above the firmament (so the Targum) against the seas below, leaning to the bounded oceans of the lower world.

themes: the sea held from the earth

schools.summary: Gill: the pillars are either the air/lower firmament quivering at thunder, or, more likely, the mountains that look like heaven's foundations and shake at God's presence in storm and earthquake.

Wesley: the mountains seem to reach and support the heavens, astonished when God rebukes men by them through thunder and earthquake; Clarke reads a poetical thunder or earthquake, tracing the mountains-as-pillars belief (Atlas, Silius Italicus).

Ellicott: storm and tempest are in view; Keil and Delitzsch: the towering mountains are 'pillars of heaven,' 'tremble' a violent to-and-fro, the 'reproof' the divine command that binds or looses nature.
Gill offers many senses for 'divideth the sea' — creation's separation, the seas and channels of commerce, the Red Sea for Israel, or the waves furrowed by a stormy wind (Jarchi).
Clarke: a manifest allusion to the Red Sea and Pharaoh, 'the proud' being Rahab, a name for Egypt (Isa. 51:9; Calmet) — from which he concludes Job was written long after Moses, near Solomon's day.

Ellicott: 'divideth' means either stirring up or calming, and 'the proud' (Rahab) if it is Egypt points to the Exodus and bears on the date of Job; Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain sense — God rouses the sea and breaks the proud one.
Henry holds both: God divides the sea and smites its proud waves by storm (Ps. 89:9-10), while those who date Job at or after Moses may read the Red Sea and drowned Egypt, Rahab being often Egypt.

debates.question: Is 'the proud' (Rahab) that God smites the raging sea, or historic Egypt at the Red Sea?

sides.position: historic Egypt and the Exodus deliverance, implying a post-Mosaic date for Job
the raging sea and its proud waves, subdued by God's power

themes: the proud waves or proud Egypt
the date of the book of Job

schools.summary: Gill reads the garnishing broadly — the visible heavens with sun, moon, stars; the invisible with angels and saints; and the church garnished with the Spirit's gifts in her ministers.
Henry: by his Spirit God has not only made but beautified the heavens (Ps. 33:6); the crooked serpent he leaves uncertain — Milky Way, a constellation, or the leviathan/whale (cf. Isa. 27:1).
Ellicott takes the crooked serpent for the forked lightning-flash, or the constellation of the Northern Dragon; Keil and Delitzsch render 'his hand hath formed the fugitive dragon.'

Clarke canvasses every option — the sun's zodiac path, zigzag lightning, sea-monsters/leviathan (Calmet), or Satan himself (Sherlock; LXX 'he destroyed the apostate dragon') — but presses his rule that no figure should prove a doctrine.

debates.question: What is 'the crooked serpent' that God's hand hath formed?

sides.position: the forked lightning-flash darting across the sky
a constellation — the Northern Dragon or the Milky Way
a sea-monster or leviathan of creation
Satan, the apostate dragon, overmastered by his Maker

outliers.note: Refuses to decide among lightning, zodiac, sea-monster, and Satan, drawing the rule that no metaphor or figurative expression should ever be pressed as proof of an article of faith.

themes: garnishing the heavens by his Spirit

schools.summary: Gill: 'parts' are the extremities, edges, and outlines of God's ways; if these are so marvellous, what must the whole be, beyond man's power to describe?

Wesley: but small parcels, the outside and visible work, God's power aptly likened to thunder; Clarke: 'parts' (ketsoth) an indistinct sketch, 'whisper' (shemets) opposed to 'thunder' (raam) — as whisper to thunder, so his works to Job's outline.

Keil and Delitzsch take the word for the extremest end-points of God's ways, the 'whisper' the faintest breath of a might that transcends understanding; Ellicott: we hear the faintest whisper and cannot endure the full thunder of his majesty — Job's final reply, which leaves his suffering no more intelligible nor the friends' theory more defensible.
Henry lands with Paul, sitting at the brink to adore the depth (Rom. 11:33): what we know of God is nothing to what is in God, and even the thunder of his power we cannot understand.

outliers.note: Reads the verse as Job's final verdict on the whole debate: more conscious than his friends of God's grandeur, he still cannot understand his own suffering, and they cannot explain it — he rejects their theory yet rests secure in faith.

themes: these are parts of his ways
